source.title: Minimum Path Cost in a Grid

teaching.hint: If you know the least cost to reach every cell in one row, what choices can lead to one specified cell in the next row?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: Rows form ordered layers, and the future from a cell depends only on its current value and column, so one best cost per cell suffices.
solution_outline.approach: Initialize each first-row cell with its own value. For each later row and each destination column, consider every previous-row column, adding its best cost, the value-indexed move cost, and the new cell value. Keep the minimum, then take the minimum in the final row.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: After processing a row, each stored column cost is the minimum total of any path from any first-row cell to that cell, including all visited values and moves.
solution_outline.correctness: Every path into a later-row cell comes from exactly one column of the preceding row. Replacing its prefix with a cheaper prefix ending at that predecessor cannot worsen the suffix, so the best path uses one of the stored predecessor optima. Testing all columns preserves the invariant, and choosing the best last-row endpoint gives the global answer.
solution_outline.complexity: O(m n^2) time and O(n) auxiliary space for an m-by-n grid with rolling row costs.
solution_outline.pitfall: The move-cost row is indexed by the source cell's value, not by its row or column.

source_fidelity_notes: The image example was omitted; arbitrary first/last columns, full next-row movement, value-indexed move costs, distinct-value grid, and bounds were retained.
